claim: Lenacapavir is the first capsid-targeting drug approved for medical use.
source: Lenacapavir, developed by Gilead Sciences, is the first capsid-targeting drug approved for medical use.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a factual statement about lenacapavir's regulatory status.

claim: Lenacapavir's potent antiviral activity is predominantly due to lethal hyperstabilisation of the capsid lattice and resultant loss of compartmentalisation.
source: We demonstrate that lenacapavir's potent antiviral activity is predominantly due to lethal hyperstabilisation of the capsid lattice and resultant loss of compartmentalisation.
evidence: This is the main finding of the study as stated in the abstract, supported by the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: The reverse transcribed cDNA genome is a target for innate immune sensors which unleash a potent interferon response that can suppress replication.
source: The cell is a hostile environment for HIV, as the reverse transcribed cDNA genome is a target for innate immune sensors which unleash a potent interferon response that can suppress replication (Zuliani Alvarez et al., 2022; Lahaye et al., 2013; Rasaiyaah et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The viral capsid facilitates early steps in the replication cycle by encapsulating the genome and associated viral enzymes.
source: For a productive infection to occur, the reverse transcribing genome must be trafficked through the cytoplasm, enter the nucleus and integrate into the preferred sites in the host chromatin, all while evading detection by the host cell. The viral capsid facilitates these early steps in the replication cycle by encapsulating the genome and associated viral enzymes.
evidence: This is established knowledge about HIV capsid function.

claim: The conical capsid shell is comprised of ~1500 copies of the capsid protein (CA).
source: The conical capsid shell is comprised of ~1500 copies of the capsid protein (CA), which spontaneously assemble into a lattice.
evidence: This is established knowledge about HIV capsid structure.

claim: The HIV capsid lattice consists of mostly hexamers and exactly 12 pentamers to form a closed fullerene cone.
source: This lattice consists of mostly hexamers and exactly 12 pentamers to form a closed fullerene cone (Ganser et al., 1999; Pornillos et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Uncoating proceeds through two discrete steps in vitro: capsids opening and catastrophic disassembly of the lattice by release of CA.
source: Recently, we demonstrated that uncoating proceeds through two discrete steps in vitro: capsids opening, in which the integrity of the cone is compromised and encapsidated proteins are released; and catastrophic disassembly of the lattice by release of CA (Márquez et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to the authors' previous work.

claim: The central pore is formed by a ring of positively charged arginine residues (R18 ring) at the sixfold symmetry axis in CA hexamers and at the fivefold axis in pentamers.
source: One of these is the central pore, which is formed by a ring of positively charged arginine residues (R18 ring) at the sixfold symmetry axis in CA hexamers and at the fivefold axis in pentamers (Jacques et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: IP6 is present at concentrations of ~40–50 μM in human cells.
source: It serves to recruit nucleotides required for reverse transcription and as a binding site for inositol hexakisphosphate (IP6), a metabolite present at concentrations of ~40–50 μM in human cells (Bunce et al., 1993; Letcher et al., 2008; Veiga et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: IP6 is specifically packaged into immature virions during assembly in producer cells, leading to a ≥10–fold enrichment.
source: IP6 is specifically packaged into immature virions during assembly in producer cells, leading to a ≥10–fold enrichment, and its interaction with the central pore is essential for the assembly and stability of the capsid (Dick et al., 2018; Mallery et al., 2018; Obr et al., 2021; Sowd and Aiken, 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: IP6 interaction with the central pore is essential for the assembly and stability of the capsid.
source: IP6 is specifically packaged into immature virions during assembly in producer cells, leading to a ≥10–fold enrichment, and its interaction with the central pore is essential for the assembly and stability of the capsid (Dick et al., 2018; Mallery et al., 2018; Obr et al., 2021; Sowd and Aiken, 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The central pore has been implicated in the capsid's interaction with microtubule-based motor proteins.
source: The central pore has also been implicated in the capsid's interaction with microtubule-based motor proteins (Huang et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: The cyclophilin binding loop interaction with CypA is mediated by a conserved glycine-proline motif (G89-P90).
source: This interaction is mediated by a conserved glycine-proline motif (G89-P90) that inserts into the CypA active site.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the CypA-capsid interaction.

claim: The CypA-capsid interaction is thought to include viral evasion of innate host defences.
source: The implications of this interaction are still to be fully understood, but are thought to include viral evasion of innate host defences (Kim et al., 2019; Miles et al., 2020; Rasaiyaah et al., 2013; Towers et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Fluorescently labelled CypA can be used to detect, quantify, and monitor disassembly of the CA lattice in permeabilised virions by TIRF microscopy without significantly influencing the capsid opening process.
source: By using a fluorescently labelled CypA, we found that it is possible to detect, quantify, and monitor disassembly of the CA lattice in permeabilised virions by total internal reflection fluorescence (TIRF) microscopy without significantly influencing the capsid opening process.
evidence: This claim is supported by the authors' previous work and is used as a method in the current study.

claim: The FG-binding site is a hydrophobic pocket in the CA N-terminal domain situated near the intra-hexameric junction between CA molecules.
source: The third host-interaction surface, the FG-binding site, is a hydrophobic pocket in the CA N-terminal domain situated near the intra-hexameric junction between CA molecules (Figure 1).
evidence: This is established knowledge about capsid structure, with reference to Figure 1 showing the binding site.

claim: The FG-binding site serves as the binding interface for Sec24C, NUP153, other nucleoporins, and CPSF6.
source: This site serves as the binding interface for several host factors, including the cytoplasmic protein Sec24C (Rebensburg et al., 2021), components of the nuclear pore complex including NUP153 (Matreyek et al., 2013) and other permeability barrier-forming nucleoporins (Dickson et al., 2024; Fu et al., 2024), and the nuclear protein CPSF6 (Bhattacharya et al., 2014; Price et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Sequential interactions with Sec24C, NUP153, nucleoporins, and CPSF6 are crucial for nuclear entry and correct integration site targeting.
source: Sequential interactions with these proteins are crucial for nuclear entry and correct integration site targeting (Bejarano et al., 2019; Saito et al., 2016; Schaller et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Host factors interact with the capsid via a phenylalanine-glycine (FG) motif.
source: Each of these proteins interacts with the capsid via a phenylalanine-glycine (FG) motif.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the interaction mechanism.

claim: Several generations of antiviral compounds target the FG-binding site by effectively mimicking the FG-motif.
source: Additionally, several generations of antiviral compounds also target this site by effectively mimicking the FG-motif (Price et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: BI-2 has a relatively small binding footprint on the CA N-terminal domain, barely extending beyond the FG-binding pocket.
source: BI-2 has a relatively small binding footprint on the CA N-terminal domain, barely extending beyond the FG-binding pocket (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by reference to Figure 1A showing the binding mode.

claim: BI-2 has a KD of 1.2 μM and IC50 of 3 μM.
source: This limited interaction is reflected in the relatively weak binding affinity (KD = 1.2 μM) and high drug concentration required to inhibit infection by 50% during the early stage of infection (half maximal inhibitory concentration, IC50=3 μM) (Price et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: PF74 extends its interaction beyond the FG-binding pocket to make additional contacts with a neighbouring CA molecule.
source: PF74, on the other hand, extends its interaction beyond the FG-binding pocket to make additional contacts with a neighbouring CA molecule (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by reference to Figure 1B showing the binding mode.

claim: PF74's bridging contacts are thought to be responsible for its 10-fold tighter KD (120 nM) and IC50 relative to BI-2.
source: These bridging contacts are thought to be responsible for PF74's 10-fold tighter KD (120 nM) and IC50 (relative to BI-2).
evidence: This is an inference based on structural data and binding measurements.

claim: Both BI-2 and PF74 can compete with host cofactor binding (Sec24C, Nup153, and CPSF6).
source: Both BI-2 and PF74 can compete with host cofactor binding (Sec24C, Nup153, and CPSF6) (Fricke et al., 2014; Matreyek et al., 2013; Peng et al., 2014; Price et al., 2014; Rebensburg et al., 2021), and also directly affect capsid structure and stability.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Both BI-2 and PF74 have capsid-opening activity.
source: While both compounds have capsid-opening activity (Bhattacharya et al., 2014; Fricke et al., 2014; Shi et al., 2011), leading to a block of reverse transcription (Jennings et al., 2020; Mallery et al., 2018; Sowd et al., 2021), PF74 also increases the stiffness of the capsid (Rankovic et al., 2018) and stabilises hexameric CA lattices (Bhattacharya et al., 2014; Mallery et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: PF74 increases the stiffness of the capsid and stabilises hexameric CA lattices.
source: While both compounds have capsid-opening activity (Bhattacharya et al., 2014; Fricke et al., 2014; Shi et al., 2011), leading to a block of reverse transcription (Jennings et al., 2020; Mallery et al., 2018; Sowd et al., 2021), PF74 also increases the stiffness of the capsid (Rankovic et al., 2018) and stabilises hexameric CA lattices (Bhattacharya et al., 2014; Mallery et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: LEN is approved by the European Union and by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration for clinical use in patients with multidrug-resistant HIV-1 infection.
source: In contrast to BI-2 and PF74, which have found use exclusively in the laboratory, LEN is a first-in-class HIV-1 capsid inhibitor in clinical trials and approved by the European Union and by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration for clinical use in patients with multidrug-resistant HIV-1 infection (Dvory-Sobol et al., 2022; Patel et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: LEN makes extensive contacts across two neighbouring CA monomers.
source: Structurally, LEN makes extensive contacts across two neighbouring CA monomers (Figure 1C), allowing for a very high-affinity interaction (KD = 215 pM).
evidence: This is supported by reference to Figure 1C showing the binding mode.

claim: LEN has a KD of 215 pM.
source: Structurally, LEN makes extensive contacts across two neighbouring CA monomers (Figure 1C), allowing for a very high-affinity interaction (KD = 215 pM).
evidence: This is established knowledge from published structural studies.

claim: LEN interferes with early and late phases of the HIV-1 replication cycle at low and high pM concentrations, respectively.
source: It interferes with early and late phases of the HIV-1 replication cycle at low and high pM concentrations, respectively, making it orders of magnitude more potent than PF74 and BI-2 (Bester et al., 2020; Link et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Integration of HIV-1 DNA into host chromatin is inhibited most potently by LEN at <500 pM.
source: Successive post-entry steps differ in their sensitivity to the drug (Bester et al., 2020; Link et al., 2020), whereby integration of HIV-1 DNA into host chromatin is inhibited most potently (<500 pM), followed by nuclear import and reverse transcription, which is inhibited at high pM (Sowd et al., 2021) to low nM LEN (Bester et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: LEN increased the number of viral cores in the cytoplasm in a dose-dependent manner.
source: Remarkably, imaging studies (Bester et al., 2020) and biochemical assays (Selyutina et al., 2022) showed that LEN increased the number of viral cores in the cytoplasm in a dose-dependent manner.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: LEN breaks IP6-stabilised capsids while preventing disassembly of CA lattices with open edges.
source: Here, we have used single-molecule fluorescence imaging to show that LEN breaks IP6-stabilised capsids while preventing disassembly of CA lattices with open edges.
evidence: This is a main finding of the study supported by the experimental data presented.

claim: Capsid breakage by LEN depends on the occupancy of FG binding pockets.
source: Indirect visualisation of LEN binding to authentic capsids in real time reveals that capsid breakage depends on the occupancy of FG binding pockets.
evidence: This is a main finding of the study supported by the experimental data presented.

claim: LEN and IP6 synergise to accelerate CA assembly but promote tubular (LEN) versus conical (IP6) structures.
source: In vitro assembly assays show that LEN and IP6 synergise to accelerate CA assembly but promote tubular (LEN) versus conical (IP6) structures, leading to the formation of aberrant capsid structures.
evidence: This is a main finding of the study supported by the experimental data presented.

claim: Substoichiometric binding of LEN stabilises the hexameric CA lattice at the cost of fully closed capsids, leading to loss of reverse transcription.
source: Altogether, our data suggest that substoichiometric binding of LEN stabilises the hexameric CA lattice at the cost of fully closed capsids, leading to loss of reverse transcription.
evidence: This is a main conclusion of the study based on the experimental data presented.

claim: The LEN mechanism becomes dominant in the high pM range, close to the IC95 of viral replication.
source: This mechanism becomes dominant in the high pM range, close to the inhibitory concentration that leads to 95% inhibition (IC95) of viral replication.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data presented.

claim: Virions with a 'leaky' capsid lost their entire GFP signal in a single step upon membrane permeabilisation.
source: Upon membrane permeabilisation, virions with a 'leaky' capsid lost their entire GFP signal in a single step (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Virions containing an intact capsid retained the pool of GFP inside the capsid after membrane permeabilisation.
source: In contrast, virions containing an intact capsid retained the pool of GFP inside the capsid.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: The residual GFP signal in intact capsids was lost in a second step upon spontaneous loss of capsid integrity.
source: This residual (low intensity) GFP signal was lost in a second step upon spontaneous loss of capsid integrity (Figure 2B, 'opening'), whereby the lifetime of each opening capsid was given by the time difference between the two GFP release steps.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: A subset of GFP-containing capsids remained closed at the end of the 30-min experiment.
source: A subset of GFP-containing capsids remained at the end of the experiment (Figure 2B, 'closed'), because the 30-min imaging period was not long enough to observe opening of all capsids.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Virus preparations contained a subset of immature particles where GFP remains bound to the viral membrane as part of the immature Gag lattice.
source: Finally, virus preparations also contained a subset of immature particles that remain at the initial high intensity level throughout the imaging period because the GFP remains bound to the viral membrane as part of the immature Gag lattice (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: In the presence of 500 nM LEN, the AF568-CypA signal of capsids that were defective or started to uncoat remained constant.
source: Second, the AF568-CypA signal of capsids that were defective to begin with (Figure 2C, 'leaky') or started to uncoat (Figure 2C, 'opening') remained constant.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: 500 nM LEN treatment caused earlier release of the encapsidated GFP.
source: First, LEN treatment caused earlier release of the encapsidated GFP (Figure 2C, 'opening'), resulting in a faster decaying survival curve (Figure 2D, light green line) and a concomitant threefold decrease in the fraction of closed capsids at the end of the experiment.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figures 2C and 2D.

claim: LEN binding induces rupture of capsids but prevents the loss of CA subunits from defective or ruptured capsids.
source: Taken together, the GFP release and CypA paint analysis in the presence of 500 nM LEN suggest that binding of LEN induces rupture of capsids (leading to early GFP release) but prevents the loss of CA subunits from defective or ruptured capsids (stable CypA paint signal).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data presented in Figure 2.

claim: LEN dose-dependently accelerates capsid opening kinetics with maximal effect at ≥50 nM LEN.
source: The survival curves (Figure 3A) showed a pronounced concentration-dependent acceleration of capsid opening kinetics with an intermediate effect at 5 nM and the maximal effect at ≥50 nM LEN, leading to a two- to fourfold (5 nM and ≥50 nM LEN, respectively) decrease in the fraction of capsids that remained closed after 15 min (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figures 3A and 3C.

claim: LEN increased the fraction of particles with leaky capsids from 56 ± 5% (no drug) to 65 ± 7% (500 nM LEN).
source: Similarly, we observed a concentration-dependent increase in the fraction of particles with leaky capsids from 56 ± 5% (no drug) to 65 ± 7% (500 nM LEN) (Figure 3—figure supplement 3), which we attribute to rapid drug-induced capsid rupture that occurred before membrane permeabilisation.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: LEN concentrations of ≥50 nM prevented disassembly of leaky and opening capsids.
source: Next, we analysed the CypA paint signal to determine the effect of LEN on the lattice after capsid integrity loss. LEN concentrations of ≥50 nM prevented disassembly of leaky and opening capsids, as evidenced by the stable CypA paint signal (Figure 3D), which persisted for at least 5 h (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figures 3D and 3E.

claim: 2–4 LEN molecules per hexamer are sufficient to prevent the release of CA subunits from a CA lattice with open edges.
source: Based on these considerations, we estimate that 2–4 LEN molecules per hexamer are sufficient to prevent the release of CA subunits from a CA lattice with open edges.
evidence: This is a calculation based on the experimental data and occupancy estimates.

claim: IP6 (100 μM) strongly stabilised capsids in permeabilised virions, leading to reduced capsid opening kinetics.
source: As before, IP6 (100 μM) strongly stabilised capsids in permeabilised virions, leading to reduced capsid opening kinetics (Figure 3B) and a ~twofold increase in the fraction of closed capsids at 15 min compared to the control without IP6 (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figures 3B and 3C.

claim: IP6 partially counteracted the capsid-breaking effect at 5 nM LEN.
source: IP6 partially counteracted the capsid-breaking effect at 5 nM LEN (compare Figure 3A and B), but even at this concentration the drug increased capsid opening kinetics relative to IP6 only (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figures 3A and 3B.

claim: At high LEN concentrations (≥50 nM), IP6 was no longer able to slow the premature rupture of the capsid induced by the drug.
source: At high LEN concentrations (≥50 nM), the survival curves measured in the presence and absence of IP6 were essentially the same, showing that IP6 was no longer able to slow the premature rupture of the capsid induced by the drug (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: IP6 partially protects capsids from LEN-induced structural damage, but only at low drug concentrations.
source: We conclude that IP6 partially protects capsids from LEN-induced structural damage, but only at low drug concentrations.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data presented in Figure 3.

claim: Preincubation with 5 nM LEN for 4 hr increased the extent of drug-induced capsid rupture to that observed at 500 nM without preincubation.
source: To test this, we preincubated virions with 5 nM LEN for 4 hr, during which 95% of sites are occupied. Analysis of GFP release traces showed that preincubation with 5 nM LEN increased the extent of drug-induced capture rupture to that observed at 500 nM without preincubation (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: A CPSF6 peptide (CPSF6p, residues 313–327) with a C-terminal cysteine labelled with a fluorescent dye binds with a half-life of 11 s to the capsids of permeabilised virions.
source: A CPSF6 peptide (CPSF6p, residues 313–327) with a C-terminal cysteine labelled with a fluorescent dye fulfilled these criteria, binding with a half-life of 11 s to the capsids of permeabilised virions on the TIRF microscope coverslip (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: At 200 nM CPSF6p paint probe concentration, ~40 labelled CPSF6p are bound at equilibrium per capsid, occupying <3% of FG binding pockets.
source: At the CPSF6p paint probe concentration (200 nM) used in the LEN binding assay, ~40 labelled CPSF6p are bound at equilibrium per capsid, occupying <3% of FG binding pockets.
evidence: This is a measurement from the experimental data.

claim: The association rate constant for LEN binding to authentic HIV capsids is kon = 1.84 ± 0.78×10^5 M^–1 s^–1.
source: The association rate constant determined from the pooled data of both experiments (kon = 1.84 ± 0.78×105 M–1 s–1, Figure 4D) was within a factor of three of the published value (kon = 6.5 ± 0.3×104 M–1 s–1), while the KD of 0.51±0.58 nM was about two times the published value (KD = 0.24 ± 0.09 nM; Link et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a measurement from the experimental data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The KD for LEN binding to authentic HIV capsids is 0.51±0.58 nM.
source: The association rate constant determined from the pooled data of both experiments (kon = 1.84 ± 0.78×105 M–1 s–1, Figure 4D) was within a factor of three of the published value (kon = 6.5 ± 0.3×104 M–1 s–1), while the KD of 0.51±0.58 nM was about two times the published value (KD = 0.24 ± 0.09 nM; Link et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a measurement from the experimental data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The stability of IP6-responsive capsids in the absence of drug exceeded the level of IP6-mediated stabilisation previously observed, with little or no loss of capsids over the 90-min imaging period.
source: Remarkably, the stability of the IP6-responsive capsids in the absence of drug exceeded the level of IP6-mediated stabilisation we have previously observed, and we observed little or no loss of capsids over the 90-min imaging period (Figure 4F, 0 nM LEN).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: The half-life of IP6-stabilised capsids in the new assay design is on the order of day(s).
source: The same observation held when imaging was extended to 8 hr, and we estimate the half-life of IP6-stabilised capsids in this assay design to be on the order of day(s).
evidence: This is an estimate based on the experimental data.

claim: Rupture of IP6-stabilised capsids accelerated with increasing LEN concentrations, with half-life decreasing from 4.5 hr at 0.2 nM to 1 hr at 1 nM.
source: Firstly, rupture of IP6-stabilised capsids accelerated with increasing LEN concentrations. This is apparent from the concentration-dependent faster decay of the survival curves and the corresponding decrease of the half-life of the intact capsid (Figure 4G, note the log-log scale) from 4.5 hr at 0.2 nM to 1 hr at 1 nM, with rupture becoming essentially immediate at >20 nM LEN (half-life of 2–3 min).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figures 4F and 4G.

claim: The overall efficiency of capsid rupture decreased sharply toward the lower end of the LEN concentration range, dropping below 65% at 0.4 nM LEN.
source: Thirdly, the overall efficiency of capsid rupture decreased sharply toward the lower end of the concentration range, dropping below 65% at 0.4 nM LEN (Figure 4—figure supplement 3D).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3D.

claim: At sub-nM LEN concentrations, LEN induced breakage when 20–30% of FG sites were drug-bound.
source: At sub-nM concentrations, LEN induced breakage when 20–30% of FG sites were drug-bound.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 4H.

claim: At LEN concentrations ≥10 nM, the mean occupancy at the time of capsid breakage levelled off at ~70%.
source: At LEN concentrations ≥10 nM, the mean occupancy at the time of capsid breakage levelled off at ~70%.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 4H.

claim: Preincubation of virions with LEN for 48 hr had little effect on inhibition during the first phase of the dose-response curve (1.3-fold reduction in IC50).
source: Preincubation had little effect on inhibition during the first phase (1.3-fold reduction in IC50, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A), consistent with a block at a late stage (e.g. integration) such that the drug had sufficient time to reach the requisite occupancy irrespective of preincubation.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Preincubation with LEN reduced infection by two- to threefold at concentrations ≥0.256 nM.
source: In contrast to the modest effect at low LEN concentrations, preincubation reduced infection by two- to threefold at concentrations ≥0.256 nM (i.e. during the second inhibitory phase), whereby the IC95 was 0.5 nM and 1 nM with and without preincubation, respectively (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The IC50 for reverse transcription in Jurkat cells was 1.08 nM LEN without preincubation and 0.59 nM with 48 hr preincubation.
source: The IC50 for reverse transcription in Jurkat cells was 1.08 nM LEN without preincubation, consistent with the dose-response in CEM cells (IC50=0.68 nM; Sowd et al., 2021). This value dropped to 0.59 nM when virions were preincubated for 48 hr with LEN prior to infection.
evidence: This is a measurement from the experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The IC50 values for DNA synthesis corresponded to the IC95 values for infection.
source: Interestingly, the IC50 values for DNA synthesis corresponded to the IC95 values for infection, consistent with a second phase mechanism whereby loss of capsid integrity leads to inhibition of DNA synthesis.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data and supports the proposed mechanism.

claim: LEN inhibits a late post-entry step when binding to 15% (KD = 0.51 nM) or 30% (KD = 0.24 nM) of sites.
source: From this analysis we conclude that LEN inhibits a late post-entry step when binding to 15% (KD = 0.51 nM) or 30% (KD = 0.24 nM) of sites, but this block is insufficient to reduce infection below a level of ~10%.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data shown in Figures 5C and 5D.

claim: At 50% (KD = 0.51 nM) or 70% (KD = 0.24 nM) occupancy of sites on the CA lattice, LEN additionally blocks infection by inhibiting reverse transcription.
source: At 50% (KD = 0.51 nM) or 70% (KD = 0.24 nM) occupancy of sites on the CA lattice, LEN additionally blocks infection by inhibiting reverse transcription, ultimately reducing infection to levels below 1%.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data shown in Figures 5C and 5D.

claim: CA (75 μM) assembled with similar kinetics in the presence of 100 μM or 150 μM IP6 but did not assemble at lower IP6 concentrations.
source: First, we varied the concentration of IP6 and observed that CA (75 μM) assembled with similar kinetics in the presence of 100 μM or 150 μM IP6 but did not assemble at lower IP6 concentrations (Figure 6A, left).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Assembly products formed with only IP6 showed primarily conical shapes with dimensions similar to those observed for native HIV capsids.
source: As expected, negative stain EM images of assembly products formed with only IP6 showed primarily conical shapes with dimensions similar to those observed for native HIV capsids (Figure 6A, right).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: LEN in the presence of low IP6 promoted formation of CA tubes (often closed at their ends) with lengths of >500 nm.
source: Strikingly, LEN in the presence of low IP6 promoted formation of CA tubes (often closed at their ends) with lengths of >500 nm, while increasing IP6 concentrations biased assembly increasingly towards shorter tubes and conical shapes (Figure 6B, right).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Addition of 1–50 μM LEN increased CA assembly efficiency in a concentration-dependent manner above the level observed for IP6 only.
source: Next, we varied the concentration of LEN in the presence of 200 μM IP6. Addition of 1–50 μM LEN increased CA assembly efficiency in a concentration-dependent manner above the level observed for IP6 only (Figure 6C, left).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The highest LEN concentration (50 μM) did not promote CA (75 μM) assembly without IP6 in low salt conditions.
source: Notably, the highest LEN concentration (50 μM) did not promote CA (75 μM) assembly without IP6 in low salt conditions (Figure 6B, left).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: LEN is insufficient to promote CA assembly by itself in low salt conditions but synergises with IP6 to increase assembly kinetics and yields.
source: We conclude that LEN is insufficient to promote CA assembly by itself in low salt conditions but synergises with IP6 to increase assembly kinetics and yields.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: IP6 promotes cone assembly, whereas LEN biases assembly toward tube formation.
source: Importantly, IP6 promotes cone assembly, whereas LEN biases assembly toward tube formation such that closed tubes form in the presence of high drug and sufficiently low IP6.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Almost all LEN-treated virions (96%) contained additional CA structures next to the main capsid (61%) and/or appeared with a double layered capsid (45%).
source: In contrast to untreated virions which contained mostly single capsids comprised of a single CA layer (74%), almost all LEN-treated virions (96%) contained additional CA structures next to the main capsid (61%) and/or appeared with a double layered capsid (45%) (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is an observation from the cryoET data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: CypA paint analysis of virions pre-treated with 500 nM LEN showed an average 1.7–1.8-fold increase of the CypA paint signal.
source: CypA paint analysis of virions pre-treated with 500 nM LEN corroborated this overassembly phenotype, showing an average 1.7–1.8-fold increase of the CypA paint signal (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C–E), consistent with the presence of a larger overall CA lattice surface area.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C–E.

claim: PF74 slowed the loss of CA from leaky and opening capsids in a concentration-dependent manner.
source: PF74 slowed the loss of CA from leaky and opening capsids in a concentration-dependent manner.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Maximum stabilisation by PF74 required essentially all sites to be drug-bound (97–99% at 10 μM), but even at this occupancy ~70% signal loss was observed after 80 min.
source: Maximum stabilisation required essentially all sites to be drug-bound (97–99% at 10 μM), but even at this occupancy we observed ~70% signal loss after 80 min (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: PF74 was unable to prevent CA lattice disassembly to the same extent as LEN.
source: Thus, PF74 was unable to prevent CA lattice disassembly to the same extent as LEN (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is a comparison based on the experimental data shown in Figures 3E and 7B.

claim: 50 μM BI-2 only marginally slowed the release of CA subunits from the lattice.
source: As expected, CypA paint analysis showed that 50 μM BI-2 only marginally slowed the release of CA subunits from the lattice (Figure 7E).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: PF74 exerts the same structural effects on the capsid as LEN but less potently, while BI-2 breaks the capsid but is unable to slow subsequent disassembly.
source: These observations together with those described above suggest that PF74 exerts the same structural effects on the capsid as LEN but less potently, while BI-2 breaks the capsid but is unable to slow subsequent disassembly.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data comparing the three drugs.

claim: Late phase inhibition with PF74 required >95% occupancy.
source: Compared to LEN, the PF74 curve was shifted to higher occupancies, whereby late phase inhibition with PF74 required >95% occupancy, i.e. the same as required for stabilisation of open CA lattices (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figures 7A and 7D.

claim: LEN required between 35–70% occupancy for late phase inhibition.
source: In comparison, LEN required between 35–70% occupancy for late phase inhibition (Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B), again corresponding to the level required for CA lattice stabilisation (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figures 5C and 3E.

claim: At 100 μM, CPSF6p promoted capsid opening, but with slower kinetics than the FG pocket-binding drugs.
source: At 100 μM (twofold above the KD of 50 μM for binding to CA hexamers), CPSF6p promoted capsid opening, but with slower kinetics than the FG pocket-binding drugs (Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: 100 μM CPSF6p strongly inhibited CA release as evident from slow decay in the CypA paint signal over 80 min.
source: CypA paint analysis showed that 100 μM CPSF6p strongly inhibited CA release (Figure 8A) as evident from slow decay in the CypA paint signal over 80 min (Figure 8C).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figures 8A and 8C.

claim: 5 μM CPSF6p (18.5% occupancy) partially inhibited CA lattice dissociation.
source: Further, 1 μM CPSF6p (6% occupancy, Figure 8B) was insufficient to stabilise the lattice but 5 μM (18.5% occupancy, Figure 8B) partially and 10 μM (<50% occupancy) strongly inhibited CA lattice dissociation.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: CPSF6p was similarly stabilising relative to occupancy to LEN and more potent than PF74 and BI-2, providing partial stabilisation when fewer than 20% of binding sites are occupied.
source: Thus, CPSF6p was similarly stabilising relative to occupancy to LEN and more potent than PF74 and BI-2, providing partial stabilisation when fewer than 20% of binding sites are occupied.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data comparing CPSF6p to the drugs.

claim: The antiviral mechanism of LEN can be considered a form of 'lethal hyperstability' in which lattice stability is increased at the cost of its flexibility and ultimately capsid integrity.
source: The antiviral mechanism of LEN can therefore be considered a form of 'lethal hyperstability' in which lattice stability is increased at the cost of its flexibility and ultimately capsid integrity.
evidence: This is a conceptual interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: Efficient and rapid drug-induced capsid rupture and lattice stabilisation occurs when half of the binding sites are occupied.
source: The effects of lethal hyperstability are observable prior to reaching binding equilibrium or full occupancy and we estimate that efficient and rapid drug-induced capsid rupture and lattice stabilisation occurs when half of the binding sites are occupied.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data.

claim: BI-2 offers no potential for enhancing contacts between individual proteins within the lattice.
source: BI-2 is the simplest compound, and only makes contacts within a single monomer and has the lowest affinity. As such it offers no potential for enhancing contacts between individual proteins within the lattice.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural data and experimental observations.

claim: PF74 and LEN lock monomers together within the hexamer, potentially limiting their ability to move with respect to each other.
source: PF74 and LEN, on the other hand, both make contacts across the junction between monomers within the context of the hexamer, and both have been shown to have higher affinity for hexamers than monomers. This suggests that the two drugs lock monomers together within the hexamer, potentially limiting their ability to move with respect to each other - reducing degrees of freedom and hence flexibility within the lattice that is required to maintain a closed capsid.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural data and experimental observations.

claim: The degree of lattice stabilisation correlates with the degree to which the drugs bridge the junction between monomers.
source: The degree of lattice stabilisation, therefore, correlates with the degree to which the drugs bridge the junction between monomers.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data comparing the three drugs.

claim: LEN may result in an induced fit switch to the hexameric configuration of residues 58–61.
source: The authors speculate that LEN may result in an induced fit switch to the hexameric configuration (Schirra et al., 2023), and our data would be consistent with such a model.
evidence: This is speculation from cited literature that is consistent with the current findings.

claim: LEN restricts CA flexibility, causing a build-up of lattice strain, and consequently lattice fracture.
source: The authors proposed that the compound restricts CA flexibility, causing a build-up of lattice strain, and consequently lattice fracture.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism from cited literature that is consistent with the current findings.

claim: IP6 plays a critical role for the formation of pentamers and high curvature.
source: Finally, cryoEM of templated CA lattices confirmed that LEN binds exclusively to hexamers and suggested a critical role of IP6 for the formation of pentamers and high curvature (Highland et al., 2023), consistent with our observation that IP6 can partially antagonise LEN-induced rupture of the closed cone.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature and is consistent with the current findings.

claim: LEN and the closely related analogue GS-CA1 lead to the formation of aberrant capsids in virions.
source: This is consistent with the observation that LEN (Bester et al., 2020) and the closely related analogue GS-CA1 (Yant et al., 2019) lead to the formation of aberrant capsids in virions.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: IP6 binds to the electropositive 'pore' created by 6 (or 5) copies of Arg18 at the centre of each CA hexamer (or pentamer).
source: IP6 binds to the electropositive 'pore' created by 6 (or 5) copies of Arg18 at the centre of each CA hexamer (or pentamer).
evidence: This is established knowledge about IP6 binding.

claim: IP6 is thought to be particularly important for incorporation of pentamers required for forming the high curvature lattice at the ends of the cone.
source: By neutralising the charge repulsion, IP6 stabilises these structures and is thought to be particularly important for incorporation of pentamers (Gupta et al., 2022; Renner et al., 2021) required for forming the high curvature lattice at the ends of the cone.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: LEN drives assembly of low curvature hexameric lattices.
source: On the other hand, LEN drives assembly of low curvature hexameric lattices (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The high-dose phase of LEN inhibition occurs above 0.5 nM LEN.
source: The high-dose phase occurs above 0.5 nM LEN, above which the considerations of capsid rupture are relevant.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data.

claim: Loss of reverse transcription accompanies the high-dose phase of LEN inhibition.
source: The high-dose phase also corresponds to the concentrations at which reverse transcription is also inhibited.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: Loss of RT activity is attributed to the opening of the capsid lattice and release of the RT enzyme.
source: We and others had previously attributed the loss of reverse transcriptase activity to the opening of the capsid lattice and release of the RT enzyme (Christensen et al., 2020; Jennings et al., 2020; Sowd et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: LEN exerts its effects at much lower capsid occupancy than PF74.
source: However, LEN is not simply a tighter-binding version of PF74. Figure 5C (LEN) and Figure 7D (PF74) show that when the drug response curves are plotted as a function of occupancy, LEN exerts its effects at much lower capsid occupancy than PF74.
evidence: This is a comparison based on the experimental data shown in Figures 5C and 7D.

claim: Increased CA affinity only partially explains LEN's superior potency.
source: This suggests that increased CA affinity only partially explains LEN's superior potency and may speak to a greater 'rigidification potential' or ultrastructure-altering capability relative to prior compounds that target this same site.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data.

claim: At its EC50, LEN occupies approximately 15-30% of the FG-binding sites, while PF74 occupies >80% of sites.
source: Our data predict that, at its EC50, LEN occupies approximately 15-30% of the FG-binding sites, while PF74 occupies >80% of sites (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is a calculation based on the experimental data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: CPSF6 binds via a linear peptide motif and, like PF74 and LEN, makes contacts across the junction between monomers.
source: The best characterised of the cofactors interacting with the FG pocket is CPSF6, which binds via a linear peptide motif and, like PF74 and LEN, makes contacts across the junction between monomers.
evidence: This is established knowledge about CPSF6 binding.

claim: CryoET imaging of CA cones showed that CPSF6 binding is independent of lattice curvature while PF74 prefers low curvature regions.
source: Indeed, cryoET imaging of CA cones have shown that CPSF6 binding is independent of lattice curvature (Stacey et al., 2023) while PF74 prefers low curvature regions (Lu, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Endogenous CPSF6 will likely have a higher binding constant due to avidity, as it is expected to be at least a dimer.
source: We acknowledge that we are studying an isolated monomeric peptide motif, while endogenous CPSF6 will likely have a higher binding constant due to avidity, as it is expected to be at least a dimer (Ning et al., 2018), but possibly higher, as CPSF6 has been associated with phase separated condensates within the nucleus (Greig et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The nuclear localisation of CPSF6 and its stabilisation activity may account for the observation of capsid remnants in the nucleus discrete from integrated proviral DNA.
source: The nuclear localisation of CPSF6 and the above stabilisation activity may account for the observation of capsid remnants in the nucleus discrete from integrated proviral DNA (Müller et al., 2021; Zila et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature and is consistent with the current findings.

claim: LEN functions by lethal hyperstabilisation, and this is a powerful mechanism for achieving multi-log impacts on viral infectivity.
source: Our work here shows that LEN functions by lethal hyperstabilisation, and that this is a powerful mechanism for achieving multi-log impacts on viral infectivity.
evidence: This is a main conclusion of the study based on the experimental data.

claim: LEN reveals that FG-pocket binding can drastically alter the capsid integrity.
source: Furthermore, LEN reveals that FG-pocket binding can drastically alter the capsid integrity.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data.
